name: Ubuntu
era: An old ethic, named in writing since the 19th century

quote.text: A person is a person through other persons.

quotes.text: My humanity is caught up, is inextricably bound up, in yours.
I am because we are; and since we are, therefore I am.
To be free is not merely to cast off one’s chains, but to live in a way that respects and enhances the freedom of others.
In time we shall be in a position to bestow upon South Africa the greatest gift possible: a more human face.
Without forgiveness there is no future.

Used respectfully for any older woman.

practices.name: Greet someone fully
practices.instructions: With the first people you meet today, stop walking. Look at them, greet them by name, ask how they are and wait for the answer. Then say how you are. Only after that move on to whatever you needed. Do the same for people you usually pass without a word: the cleaner, the bus driver, the neighbour.
practices.why: In Zulu the greeting sawubona means "we see you". Across southern Africa, to begin with business before greeting is to treat a person as a means.
variations: Greet every person in a room before you sit down.
Learn one colleague’s family members’ names.
Greet in isiZulu or Sesotho if you are with speakers who welcome it.

practices.name: Call or visit one person
practices.instructions: Choose one person: a relative, an old friend, someone who is ill or alone. Call or go in person; do not text. Ask after them and their family, and listen. Do not bring your own agenda. If they need something you can do, do it.
practices.why: A person becomes a person through relationships, and relationships are kept alive by turning up. Presence is the currency of ubuntu.
variations: Visit an elder and ask for a story.
Call someone you have fallen out with.
Sit with someone who is grieving, without needing to say anything.

practices.name: Cook or eat with others
practices.instructions: Eat your evening meal with at least one other person. Cook enough for one more than you expect. Serve others before yourself, eldest first. Keep phones off the table. If you live alone, invite someone, or carry a plate next door.
practices.why: The proverb says a guest’s stomach is small: there is always enough to share. In much of Africa eating alone when others are near is close to an offence.
variations: Cook one pot and eat from the centre.
Take food to someone who cannot cook for themselves.
Host a meal where everyone brings one dish.

practices.name: Act of service
practices.instructions: Do one useful thing for your household, street or community that is nobody’s job in particular: carry, fix, clean, mind a child, give a lift. Do it without being asked and without mentioning it.
practices.why: Ubuntu is judged by conduct. Of a generous, dependable person, people say that she has ubuntu.
variations: Join a neighbour’s task as an extra pair of hands.
Give time to a local organisation.

practices.name: Listen without fixing
practices.instructions: Ask one person how they really are, then listen for ten minutes. Do not give advice, tell your own story or look at your phone. When they stop, ask: "What else?" At the end, say one thing you heard that mattered to you.
practices.why: Ubuntu holds that a person becomes a person through other people. Being heard is one of the oldest ways of being made more human.
variations: Do it with someone you rarely listen to.
Do it as a daily habit with the same person.

rules.why: The person comes before the business. A request without a greeting is rude everywhere ubuntu is practised.

rules.text: Do not eat alone if you can help it
rules.why: Food is the simplest thing to share, and sharing it is how strangers become people to each other.

rules.text: Ask how we are, not how I am
rules.why: In many southern African languages you ask after the whole household, and you answer for yours.
Ukuhlonipha. Age is honoured because experience is a resource the community holds in common.
For funerals, weddings, illness and trouble. Presence matters more than the right words, and it is usually the harder part.
If you wronged someone today, go to them. Restoring the relationship is the point, not being right.

ethics.title: Dignity of every person
ethics.text: Each person has a worth that does not depend on usefulness, status or behaviour. South Africa’s highest court has read ubuntu into the meaning of human dignity.
ethics.practice: Give your full attention today to someone the world usually overlooks.

ethics.title: Restore, do not just punish
ethics.text: When harm is done the aim is to mend the relationship and bring the offender back into the community. Justice is repair.
ethics.practice: With one person who wronged you, ask what would actually mend it.

ethics.title: Hospitality as duty
ethics.text: A stranger is a person through whom you become one. Feeding and sheltering a traveller is not optional.
ethics.practice: Offer something, tea, food, a seat, to someone you were not expecting.

ethics.title: Generosity
ethics.text: What you have is held partly in trust for others. The person praised for ubuntu is the one who shares.
ethics.practice: Give something today that you will actually notice the lack of.

ethics.title: Solidarity
ethics.text: Your neighbour’s trouble is yours. You go, you carry, you contribute, without waiting to be asked.
ethics.practice: Find out who near you is having a hard time, and turn up.

ethics.title: Respect for elders and ancestors
ethics.text: Those who came before made your life possible and remain part of the community.
ethics.practice: Ask an older relative for a story about someone you never met.

philosophy.title: Relational personhood
philosophy.text: You are not first an individual who then chooses relationships. You become a person in and through them. "I am because we are."
philosophy.practice: List the people without whom you would not be who you are.

philosophy.title: Community before individual
philosophy.text: The good of the group and the good of the person are not rivals. A person thrives when the community does, and is diminished when others are.
philosophy.practice: In one decision today, ask what serves "us".

philosophy.title: Forgiveness frees both
philosophy.text: To forgive is not to forget or excuse. It is to refuse to let the wrong define either of you, and it releases the forgiver first.
philosophy.practice: Name one resentment you are carrying and what it costs you.

philosophy.title: Consensus
philosophy.text: Decisions are talked through until everyone can live with them. The elders sit under the tree until they agree.
philosophy.practice: In a disagreement, keep talking past the point where you would normally vote or leave.

philosophy.title: Personhood is achieved
philosophy.text: One can be more or less of a person. Cruelty and selfishness diminish it. Of someone who acts inhumanly people say: he is not a person.
philosophy.practice: What did you do today that made you more of a person?

philosophy.title: Seeing and being seen
philosophy.text: A greeting acknowledges that the other exists and matters. To be ignored is a small death.
philosophy.practice: Notice who you do not see.

philosophy.title: The living, the dead and the unborn
philosophy.text: The community extends in time. You answer to ancestors and you hold the world in trust for those to come.
philosophy.practice: What were you handed that you must hand on?

philosophy.title: A more human face
philosophy.text: Steve Biko held that Africa’s gift to the world would be in human relationships, where the industrial world had excelled in technology.
philosophy.practice: Where in your life has efficiency replaced a relationship?

philosophy.title: Interdependence is strength
philosophy.text: Needing others is not weakness. It is the human condition, and pretending otherwise is the weakness.
philosophy.practice: Ask for help with one thing today.

philosophy.title: Truth before reconciliation
philosophy.text: There is no shortcut to peace that goes around what was done. It has to be told and heard first.
philosophy.practice: Is there a truth you owe someone before things can be right?

guide.era: An old ethic, named in writing since the 19th century
intro: Ubuntu is a word from the Nguni languages of southern Africa for the quality of being human. It is usually explained with a proverb: umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu, a person is a person through other persons.

It is not a doctrine with a founder or a book. It is an ethic carried in proverbs, greetings, customs and the judgement people pass on one another’s conduct. The same idea appears under other names among neighbouring peoples: botho in Sesotho and Setswana, hunhu in Shona, and related notions across Bantu-speaking Africa. To say that someone "has ubuntu" is high praise. It means they are generous, hospitable, compassionate, and aware that their own humanity is bound up with everyone else’s.

The claim underneath is about what a person is. In much European philosophy the individual comes first: I think, therefore I am. The Kenyan theologian John Mbiti summed up the African alternative in 1969: I am because we are, and since we are, therefore I am. On this view you are not born a complete person who later enters into relationships. You become one, through family, community, the dead who came before and the unborn you are responsible to.

From that follow practical consequences. Greeting matters, because a greeting acknowledges that the other person exists. Sharing food is expected. A neighbour’s funeral is your business. Decisions are talked through until there is agreement, not carried by a bare majority. And when someone does wrong, the aim is to repair the damage and bring them back, since casting a person out diminishes everyone.

The world came to know the word in the 1990s. South Africa’s first democratic constitution invoked "a need for ubuntu but not for victimisation". The new Constitutional Court relied on it in abolishing the death penalty in 1995. And Archbishop Desmond Tutu made it the moral foundation of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which offered amnesty in exchange for full disclosure of the crimes of the apartheid era. Tutu wrote: a person with ubuntu is open and available to others, affirming of others, and does not feel threatened that others are able and good.

Ubuntu has also been turned into a slogan, a software brand and a management seminar, and South African writers have warned against a romantic version that ignores how hard it is. This Onda keeps it concrete: greet people properly, visit, eat together, serve. It is written from African sources and should be reviewed by people who grew up inside the tradition before release.

history.detail: Proverbs, praise poetry, greetings and customary law pass the idea down among Nguni, Sotho-Tswana, Shona and neighbouring peoples.

The earliest written use found so far, by the researcher Christian Gade, is in a missionary text of 1846, where it names a human quality. The proverb "a person is a person through other persons" became the standard explanation of the word only in the 1990s.
Enoch Sontonga’s hymn, "God bless Africa", is later adopted by the African National Congress.
The National Party government classifies South Africans by race and separates them in every area of life: a system built on denying that people belong to one another.

history.what: Ubuntu is written about as a philosophy
history.detail: Jordan Ngubane and others set it out in essays and novels as a distinctively African humanism.

history.what: Mbiti publishes African Religions and Philosophy
history.detail: His formula, "I am because we are", becomes the most quoted statement of African communal thought.
His essays, published the next year, argue that Africa’s contribution to the world will be to give it a more human face.
At Zimbabwe’s independence the Samkanges publish the first book to present ubuntu as a political philosophy.
Released on 11 February after twenty-seven years, he calls for negotiation and not revenge.
The interim constitution’s closing words call for understanding and not vengeance, reparation and not retaliation, ubuntu and not victimisation. The first democratic election is held in April 1994.
In S v Makwanyane the Constitutional Court rules capital punishment unconstitutional. Several justices ground the decision in ubuntu.
Chaired by Tutu, it hears more than twenty thousand statements from victims and receives some seven thousand amnesty applications. It delivers its report in October 1998.
Tutu’s account of the commission carries the word around the world.

history.what: A free operating system takes the name
history.detail: Ubuntu Linux, founded by the South African Mark Shuttleworth, is released.

concepts.text: Being a person is something achieved in relationship.
concepts.detail: The philosopher Ifeanyi Menkiti put it sharply: in African thought, personhood is something at which one can fail. It is earned by taking part in community and meeting one’s obligations.

concepts.text: The community is prior to the individual, without erasing them.
concepts.detail: Critics inside the tradition, such as Kwame Gyekye, argue for a "moderate" version in which individual rights still count. The debate is a live one.

concepts.text: Every person has worth by being a person.
concepts.detail: Justice Mokgoro wrote that ubuntu "envelops the key values of group solidarity, compassion, respect, human dignity, conformity to basic norms and collective unity".

concepts.text: Wrongdoing breaks relationships, and justice mends them.
concepts.detail: Customary courts aimed at reconciliation and compensation over punishment. The Truth Commission applied the same logic on a national scale.
Tutu insisted it is not weakness or forgetting. It requires the truth to be told, and it serves the one who forgives as much as the one forgiven.

concepts.text: Agreement reached by talking it through.
concepts.detail: Mandela described watching the regent’s court as a boy: everyone who wished to speak did so, and the meeting continued until some kind of consensus was reached.

concepts.text: The stranger is to be welcomed and fed.
concepts.detail: Mandela explained ubuntu with a traveller who stops at a village and does not have to ask for food or water.

concepts.text: The dead remain members of the community.
concepts.detail: They are remembered, consulted and honoured, and the living are answerable to them.
In Sotho and Zulu thought, how you live builds or shrinks a moral force others can feel.

concepts.text: Ubuntu can be romanticised or misused.
concepts.detail: It has been invoked to demand conformity, to silence dissent and to sell things. Its serious defenders treat it as a demanding standard, not a comfortable identity.

facts.text: The word Bantu, used for a family of several hundred African languages, simply means "people".
The Zulu greeting sawubona literally means "we see you".
South Africa has eleven official spoken languages, and its national anthem is sung in five of them.
The Constitutional Court of South Africa stands on the site of the Old Fort prison, where both Gandhi and Mandela were held.
Millions of South Africans belong to stokvels, rotating savings clubs whose name comes from the "stock fairs" of the nineteenth-century Eastern Cape.
The Boston Celtics adopted "Ubuntu" as their team chant in the season they won the 2008 championship.
Mandela’s clan name, Madiba, is used as a sign of affection and respect. His given name, Rolihlahla, means "pulling the branch of a tree", or troublemaker.
Tutu coined the phrase "rainbow nation" for post-apartheid South Africa.

glossary.meaning: A group of related languages and peoples including Zulu, Xhosa, Swati and Ndebele.
A related group including Sesotho, Setswana and Sepedi.
The system of legal racial segregation in South Africa from 1948 to the early 1990s.
The movement led by Steve Biko for psychological and political liberation.

sensitivity.note: Ubuntu is a living ethic of the peoples of southern Africa, not a brand or a technique. This Onda keeps to its everyday practice, greeting, visiting, sharing food and serving, and draws on African authors.
requiredCaveats: Pronunciations are approximate, and isiXhosa and isiZulu clicks cannot be shown in English spelling. Learn from speakers.
Do not romanticise: ubuntu is demanding, debated among Africans, and has also been misused.
Customs differ between peoples and families. When you are a guest, follow your hosts.
